s.en: The calculation took three days.
Ten years of records on loan from Instructor Regen, and the single page Viola had torn from the ledger.
Niko papered an entire wall of the warehouse and covered it in chalked figures.
According to the Academy's literature, a single time shard holds about two minutes.
From one month's deliveries in the ledger, they estimated the ten-year total.
"...No good. However many times I run it, it doesn't add up."
On the evening of the third day, Niko finally flung down the chalk.
"Against all the time that's gone missing, the shards account for maybe a thirtieth, however generously you count."
"A thirtieth?"
"Yep. The other twenty-nine are vanishing somewhere else."
Sera looked up at the figures covering the wall.
The orderly columns of numbers looked like a maze without an exit.
"So House Eisen is..."
"Selling shards is nothing to be proud of. But the big thief's someone else. That's what it comes to."
Just because they were selling time shards didn't mean House Eisen were the real culprits.

t: 知らせてあげたかった
s.en: She wanted to tell Viola as soon as she possibly could.
But that very Viola hadn't shown her face at the Academy today.
Tonight she was attending the council at the Great Clock Tower with her father.
"Hey, Sera."
Brushing the chalk dust off his hands, Niko spoke.
"That grey bloke said it, didn't he. 'I know who's stealing it.'"
"...Yeah."
"Maybe what he said was actually true."
Without answering, Sera touched the watch in her breast pocket.
Its backward heartbeat came faintly through to her fingertips.
On the top floor of the Great Clock Tower is a hall called the Council Chamber.
Built into the back of the giant dial, the room looked out through its half-translucent face over the whole city at dusk.
The low drone of turning gears rose ceaselessly from beneath the floor.
Around the round table sat the heads of the twelve great houses that governed Vern.
The same faces that had split again and again over how the time crystal should be handled.
The Countess Rosenberg was there too. Unnaturally youthful, as ever.
Viola waited at an angle behind her father, gripping her fan.
One by one, the names in the ledger fitted themselves onto the faces in this room.
She felt sick.
"Then let us turn to today's business."
From the chair came a voice, cracked with age but carrying well.
Rector Gregor.
An old man with a white beard, dressed in a black formal coat.
A descendant of the family that founded the Academy, he had held the Rector's chair for as long as Viola could remember.
Never without a gentle smile, he was deeply loved by the students.
"As you are all aware, the time crystal has been ailing this past month."
"The recent accident, by good fortune, cost no lives. But there is no guarantee the next will be so kind."
The Rector looked around the table.
"I therefore propose that we bring forward the Partition Plan we have long been considering, and put it into effect."
A faint murmur ran through the hall.
The Partition Plan.
Viola had never once heard the name.
She stole a glance at her father's profile. Not a flicker. He had known.
"Put simply, we divide the city in two."
At a gesture from the Rector, a three-dimensional map of Vern rose faintly over the centre of the table.
Upper ring and lower ring.
Along the boundary between them, a wall of blue light rose up.
"So long as the crystal's power is waning, it cannot go on supporting the time of the entire city."
"Then we need only narrow what it supports. Cut off the supply of time to the lower ring and redirect that share to the upper."
"And what becomes of the lower ring, once its flow of time is cut?"
Before she knew it, her mouth had moved on its own.
Twelve pairs of eyes turned to her at once.
Her father turned sharply, but Viola didn't look away.
The Rector answered in a soft voice, as if speaking to a granddaughter.
"They go to sleep, Miss Eisen. When time stops, there is no suffering. And if the crystal recovers one day, they may even wake."
"'One day.' And when would that be?"
"Well now. Ten years hence? A hundred?"
The Rector smiled gently.
"Either way, it is a necessary sacrifice if the city of Vern is to survive."
Tens of thousands of people lived in the lower ring.
Sera. Oz. Niko's family.
They meant to shut them all inside stopped time?
"I object."
Viola's voice did not shake.
"Guarding the Great Clock is the duty of House Eisen. But the Great Clock exists to protect the city. To abandon half the city and save only the clock is to get things exactly backwards."
"Viola."
Her father's voice was low and cold.
"Step back. You were not given leave to speak."
"Father—"
"I said step back."
Viola bit her lip.
From all around the hall came chilly glances and stifled laughter.
She could tell every one of them was thinking: a little girl's prattle.
"Let us honour the young lady's passion."
The Rector smoothed things over gently.
"Then we shall put it to a vote. Those in favour of carrying out the Partition Plan?"
Hands rose, one after another.
Countess Rosenberg. House Weiss. House Graf.
When the eleventh hand went up, every eye turned to the one man who had not yet moved.
Walter Eisen.
Keeper of the Great Clock. Without his vote, no one could lay a finger on the crystal.
For a long moment her father kept his eyes closed.
Then he opened them, and slowly raised his right hand.
"House Eisen... is in favour."
"Then it is decided. The partition will close at midnight, seven days from now."
Against the Rector's declaration, no one raised a voice any longer.
When the council broke up, Viola went out alone onto the tower's balcony.
Below her spread the lower ring, sinking into twilight.
Factory smoke. Lights on the canals. The steam of supper spilling from some house's window.
In seven days, every one of those lights would stop.
And her father had lent his hand to it.
Without realising, she tightened her grip on the railing.
"—Galling, isn't it."
A voice behind her — Viola spun, snapping her fan open as she turned.
At the end of the balcony, in the shadow of the dial, stood the grey man.
"...You have some nerve."
"Quiet. I've come only to talk tonight."
He spread his hands to show her. No weapon. His watch stayed tucked inside his coat.
"Your father is not the thief."
"I beg your pardon?"
"He sells the shards, yes. But under threat. Refuse, and House Eisen is stripped of the Keepership of the Great Clock."
"And by whom, pray, is he being threatened?"
Instead of answering, the man nodded towards the window of the Council Chamber.
Inside, Rector Gregor was still chatting pleasantly with a few nobles.
Seen through the glass, he was exactly as before. A gentle, refined old gentleman.
"Him. He's the one who has been devouring this city's time for these ten years — no. For a hundred."
"A hundred...?"
"He is the very man who founded the Academy a hundred years ago. No descendant."
Viola was lost for words.
A hundred years. The year the Rewinders vanished. The year carved beside Sera's mother's name.
Everything that had been scattered was being drawn onto a single thread.
"Why tell me this?"
"Once the partition closes, it will be too late. To stop it we need that girl's power, your chronomancy, and Eisen blood to open the crystal's pedestal."
"You're asking us to join forces with you?"
"Being enemies doesn't mean we cannot share an enemy."
Behind his mask, the man gave a faint laugh.
"Three nights from now, I'll be waiting at the canal warehouse. Tell the girl, and the noisy boy too."
"Wait! Who in the world are you?"
In place of a reply, a gust of wind blew.
In the space of a blink, the man was gone.
He had stopped time and left; Viola knew it.
Not even she, a chronomancer, had been able to sense the moment it happened.
Late that night, someone knocked hesitantly at the door of Milford's Clocks.
Sera threw a jacket over her nightclothes, opened the door, and stared.
"Viola...?"
Viola stood there in an evening gown with only a coat thrown over it.
Her silver hair was coming loose, her shoes muddy from the canal paths.
She had walked all the way down from the upper ring, alone.

t: お話ししておきたくて
s.en: "Forgive me for calling so late. I simply had to speak with you tonight."
Her voice was steady. But the fingers clutching the hem of her coat were trembling white.
Without a word, Sera took her hand and drew her inside.
Oz looked out from the back with a lamp, saw who it was, and raised one eyebrow.
"...The Eisen girl, is it."
"Please excuse the late hour. My name is Viola Eisen."
"Never mind the formalities. Sit. I'll make you some tea, at least."
With that gruff word, Oz withdrew to the kitchen.
Viola perched on the round stool in front of the workbench.
In the cramped shop full of clocks, she looked terribly out of place, and terribly small.
"What happened?"
One thing at a time, Viola told her what had happened in the Council Chamber over the Partition Plan.
Midnight in seven days. Her father's raised hand. And the words of the grey man on the balcony.
As the story went on, Sera's hands had somehow become fists in her lap.
Stop the lower ring.
This shop. Oz. Niko's family. All of them.
"The Rector... for a hundred years."

t: 信じきれておりません
s.en: "It's unbelievable, isn't it. I still can't quite believe it myself."
Viola looked down.
"But my father raising his hand — that much is true. Even if he was being threatened, it doesn't change the fact that he chose to abandon half the city."
From the kitchen came the sound of water coming to the boil.
Sera moved to the stool next to Viola.
"But you objected. In front of twelve grown-ups. On your own."

t: 役にも立ちませんでした
s.en: "...Much good it did."
"Whether it did any good doesn't matter."
Sera gently wrapped Viola's ice-cold hands in both of her own.
"It made me happy. That's all."
Viola's shoulders shook, just a little.
A little later Oz came back with three steaming cups on a tray, took one look at the scene in the shop, and silently set the tray on the workbench.
Then, taking only his own cup, he withdrew into the back again.
The wall clock struck midnight.
Less than seven days remained before the partition closed.
